title: Geometric Characteristics of Subproblems in Ising-Machine-Assisted Large Neighborhood Search
abstract: Large-scale quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulations of constrained combinatorial optimization problems often exceed the input-size limit of present Ising machines or suffer from degraded solution quality as the number of binary variables increases. Large neighborhood search (LNS) mitigates this difficulty by sequentially optimizing restricted subproblems, but the structural factors that distinguish subproblems beyond the number of binary variables remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, we examine vehicle routing problems and compare a construction based on the vehicle routes of the current solution, denoted by LNS-K, with a construction based on QUBO variables and constraint relations, denoted by LNS-Q, while controlling the number of binary variables in the subproblems. Under the tested conditions, LNS-K obtained shorter total distances than LNS-Q in the matched-size comparisons, and the position variance, a measure of the spatial spread of the selected customers, decreased during the iterations in LNS-K. These observations suggest that subproblem design for sequential optimization with Ising machines should consider not only subproblem size but also semantic and geometric structures inherited from the current solution.
summary: This paper investigates how to effectively use Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) with Ising machines to solve large Vehicle Routing Problems. By comparing two subproblem construction methods, LNS-K and LNS-Q, the authors demonstrate that incorporating the semantic structure of the current solution is crucial for optimization success. The findings suggest that structural information matters more than simply controlling the size of the variables fed into the quantum annealer.
main_problem: The study addresses limitations when using Ising machines for large-scale combinatorial optimization problems, specifically QUBO formulations of VRPs.
main_result: Subproblem design for sequential optimization must consider the semantic and geometric structure inherited from the current solution, not just the number of binary variables.
method: The authors compare two Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) strategies: LNS-K (based on route structure) and LNS-Q (based on QUBO variables), applied to VRPs solved via Ising machines.
model_or_system: The model is a Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) formulated as a QUBO, which is then optimized iteratively using an Ising machine framework. The comparison focuses on how the subproblem is constructed from the current solution state.
key_observables: Total distance achieved, position variance (spatial spread of selected customers), and the number of binary variables in the subproblems.
important_parameters: The size of the subproblem ($B_m$), the type of construction rule (LNS-K vs. LNS-Q), and the controlled annealing time budget for quantum annealers.
main_assumptions: The comparison is limited by matching either the number of variables or the total annealing time, not end-to-end wall-clock runtime; a causal link between geometric localization and performance improvement is not established.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate that LNS-K yields shorter total distances and shows decreasing position variance during iterations compared to LNS-Q, even when subproblem sizes are matched.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the challenge of large QUBOs for Ising machines, proposes using LNS, and then systematically compares two construction methods (LNS-K vs. LNS-Q) on VRP instances by analyzing performance metrics like distance and spatial variance.
why_interesting: While focused on optimization heuristics, the reliance on mapping complex combinatorial problems onto QUBOs solved by quantum annealers touches upon the practical application of quantum computation for hard constraint satisfaction problems relevant to many-body physics modeling.

(a) Feasible-solution probability obtained with D-Wave Advantage 4.1 for small VRP instances. (b) Normalized total dis- tance obtained with D-Wave Advantage 4.1. Fig. 2. Final total distance obtained by LNS-K and LNS-Q for a vehicle routing problem with 400 customers. LNS-K constructs a subproblem from selected vehicles and the customers visited by those vehicles in the current solution, whereas LNS-Q constructs a subproblem from QUBO variables and the associated constraints. The horizontal labels indicate K′ for LNS-K and n′ for LNS-Q. The corresponding numbers of binary variables in the subprob- lems are summarized in Table II. Although n′ allows LNS-Q to control the subproblem size more finely, LNS-K gives shorter final total distances under the tested conditions.

Fig. 3. Iterative behavior of LNS-K and LNS-Q for subproblems with the same number of binary variables. The results are for a vehicle routing prob- lem with 400 customers. Each row corresponds to K′ = 2, 3, 4, and 5 in LNS-K, and n′ in LNS-Q is chosen to match the corresponding subproblem size, as listed in Table II. (a) Total distance of the current solution. LNS-K shows faster iterative improvement than LNS-Q, especially for smaller sub- problems. (b) Position variance of the selected customer set. In LNS-K, the selected customer set becomes more spatially localized during the optimiza- tion, whereas the position variance in LNS-Q remains nearly constant.
